Long-acting injectable progestin contraception has been studied for its potential association with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes in Latino women who have a history of gestational diabetes mellitus. This was explored in a study published in Diabetes Care in 2006. 2. A comparative metabolic study evaluated the effects of different contraceptive methods, including Norplant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), low-dose oral contraceptive pills, and the copper T380A intrauterine device (IUD), in diabetic women. This research was published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology Research in 2000. 3. Self-reported changes in capillary glucose levels and insulin requirements during the menstrual cycle were documented in a study published in Diabetic Medicine in 1995. 4. A cross-over study investigated the effects of oral contraceptives on serum lipids, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, and diabetes control in diabetic women using progestogen-only and combined estrogen/progestogen contraceptives. This was published in Hormone and Metabolic Research in 1982. 5. The metabolic effects of four different oral contraceptive compounds with varying estrogen/progestogen profiles were studied in diabetic women. This research was published in Fertility and Sterility in 1986. 6. The natural history of focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) of the liver was retrospectively studied in 44 cases, as published in Gastroenterologie Clinique et Biologique in 2001. 7. The relationship between oral contraceptive use and focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver was explored in a study published in Gastroenterology in 2000. 8. A systematic review examined the use of hormonal contraceptives in women with liver tumors, as published in Contraception in 2009. 9. The effect of megestrol acetate on sickling in sickle cell disease was studied and published in the American Journal of Medical Sciences in 1973. 10. The impact of a subdermal implant containing nomegestrol acetate (Uniplant) on carbohydrate metabolism in sickle cell patients was studied and published in Contraception in 2001. 11. The effects of Depo-Provera and Microgynon on painful crises in sickle cell anemia patients were studied and published in Contraception in 1997. 12. The use of medroxyprogesterone acetate in women with homozygous sickle cell disease was explored in a study published in The Lancet in 1982. 13. Counseling and contraceptive use in women with sickle cell disease were discussed in a study published in the BMJ in 1993. 14. The use of Norplant in women with sickle cell disease was studied and published in the International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 1993. 15. Nomegestrol acetate contraceptive implant use in women with sickle cell disease was studied and published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 1998. 16. The effect of oral contraceptive pill use on red cell deformability in women with sickle cell anemia was studied and published in the British Journal of Haematology in 1999. 17. The impact of sex and contraceptive therapy on the pharmacokinetics of zidovudine in plasma and intracellular compartments was studied and published in AIDS. 18. The lack of effect of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate on the pharmacokinetics of hormonal contraceptives was studied and published in Pharmacotherapy in 2009. 19. The implementation of the Jadelle implant in women living with HIV in resource-limited settings and concerns about drug interactions leading to unintended pregnancies were discussed in a study published in AIDS in 2014. 20. The effectiveness of Depo-medroxyprogesterone acetate as contraception in women on antiretroviral therapy and the lack of clinically significant interactions were studied and published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2007. 21. Pharmacokinetic interactions between depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and combination antiretroviral therapy were studied and published in Fertility and Sterility in 2008. 22. The pharmacokinetic interaction between ethinyl estradiol, norethindrone, and darunavir with low-dose ritonavir in healthy women was studied and published in Antiviral Therapy in 2008. 23. The effect of vicriviroc, with or without ritonavir, on oral contraceptive pharmacokinetics was studied in a randomized, open-label trial published in Clinical Therapeutics in 2011. 24. The contraceptive efficacy of oral and transdermal hormones when co-administered with protease inhibitors in HIV-1-infected women was studied and published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 25. The effect of protease inhibitors on the steady-state pharmacokinetics of oral norethindrone contraception in HIV-infected women was studied and published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014. 26. The effect of raltegravir on estradiol and norgestimate plasma pharmacokinetics following oral contraceptive administration in healthy women was studied and published in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2011. 27. The lack of effect of dolutegravir on the pharmacokinetics of methadone or oral contraceptives containing norgestimate and ethinyl estradiol was presented at the 20th Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in 2013. 28. Enhanced metabolism of levonorgestrel during phenytoin treatment in a woman with Norplant implants was studied and published in Contraception in 1986. 29. The failure of Implanon contraception in a patient taking carbamazepine for epilepsy was studied and published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2006. 30. Enhanced metabolism of levonorgestrel during phenobarbital treatment and resultant pregnancy was studied and published in Pharmacotherapy in 1998. 31. Ethinyl estradiol, but not progestogens, was found to reduce lamotrigine serum concentrations in a study published in Epilepsia in 2005. 32. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If there is a risk of STI/HIV, the correct and consistent use of condoms is recommended. Condoms, when used correctly and consistently, offer one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs, including HIV. Female condoms are effective and safe but are not as widely used as male condoms in national programs. 33. Strong CYP3A4 inducers, such as rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and others, may reduce the effectiveness of ECPs. For example, rifampicin markedly decreases ulipristal acetate levels by 90% or more, which may reduce its efficacy.
